analysis.one_liner: Blocks carbon rules for power plants and strips EPA and Army Corps authority over water permits that affect mining.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, was placed on the Senate calendar the day after introduction, and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced by Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell in response to the Obama administration's plan to regulate carbon pollution from existing coal-fired power plants, this bill would have barred federal agencies from writing any power-sector carbon rule unless Congress explicitly passed one. Its second half would rewrite the Clean Water Act: EPA and the Army Corps could no longer use their 2010-2011 guidance on which streams and wetlands are protected, permits for discharges into waters would face hard deadlines after which they are automatically approved, EPA would lose its power to veto permits for mining waste dumps in streams, and federal regulators could not override state water quality decisions. It sat on the Senate calendar with no cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal-fired power plants. The bill would have blocked carbon standards for existing coal plants and made it much harder for federal agencies to block, delay, or condition water discharge permits for mining operations — including the contentious practice of mountaintop-removal mining that fills streams with mining waste. Permit applicants would have gained an automatic approval if the government missed a 270-day or two-year deadline, plus new hurdles for EPA to overcome before superseding state decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal mining companies and coal-burning utilities

how_it_helps.text: It would block any federal agency from issuing power-plant carbon pollution standards unless Congress explicitly authorized them, responding to the June 25, 2013 presidential memorandum directing EPA to regulate existing coal plants

It would forbid permit reviewers from considering EPA and Army Corps guidance on which waters the Clean Water Act protects, require permit decisions based only on formal regulations, and let an applicant operate as if its discharge permit were approved if no decision came within 270 days

It would bar the Army Corps from restricting the use of any area as a fill disposal site once a permit is issued, set hard deadlines after which permits are deemed approved and exempt from judicial review, and limit EPA's power to override state water quality determinations
It would require EPA to analyze each Clean Water Act action's effect on jobs and economic activity state by state, with hearings and notifications when losses exceed 100 jobs or $1 million in a state

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who relies on clean water downstream of mining, industrial, or construction discharges. EPA's veto authority over harmful fill permits, its guidance-based reviews of which waters qualify for protection, and its ability to tighten weak state programs would all be curtailed or removed. Communities near mountaintop-removal mines — where mining waste is dumped into stream valleys — would lose a key federal backstop, and the effective moratorium on power-plant carbon rules would shift the health costs of coal pollution onto the public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near mines and downstream water users

drawbacks.text: The bill would have barred agencies from using any non-rulemaking guidance to decide permit cases, overriding the 2010-2011 EPA/Army Corps guidance that determined which waters are protected — a move environmental reviews said weakened protection of streams and wetlands

If the Army Corps or a permitting authority missed a deadline — 270 days for discharge permits, fixed NEPA clocks of one or two years — the permit would be considered approved automatically, and Corps permits would be exempt from judicial review

Permit approvals could be based only on formal regulations, not guidance, and state water quality determinations could not be superseded by EPA, sharply limiting federal oversight of mining and industrial discharges
Even a supporter would acknowledge the bill went well beyond coal, rewriting Clean Water Act sections 402, 404, 401, and 303 nationwide and permanently, not just for coal mines

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real help to coal communities facing job losses, but it achieved that almost entirely by stripping federal safeguards from the nation's water rules and blocking carbon limits outright. The permit "deemed approved" provisions and the narrow loss thresholds (100 jobs or $1 million) would have made it hard to stop any discharge permit for any reason, and the bill did nothing to diversify coal-dependent local economies. Weakened federal clean-water enforcement would fall on everyone downstream. The honest trade-off: coal employment relief purchased by permanently lowering water and air protections for the public.

outcome.mechanism: McConnell introduced it, it was read and placed on the Senate calendar, no cosponsors ever signed on, and it never got a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2013, read the first time, and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 191)
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without the bill ever receiving a vote; the full action history shows no activity after placement on the calendar

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, EPA and the Army Corps kept the authority the bill would have removed — including EPA's power to block mining waste discharges into waters and to write carbon standards for power plants, which EPA later issued in 2015 under the Clean Air Act. The coal industry did not get the exemptions it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA, the Army Corps, and public water protections

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 17, 2013, in response to the president's directive that EPA regulate carbon pollution from existing coal plants

for.name: Coal industry and Kentucky mining interests
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed efforts to block EPA carbon and water rules affecting coal mining, the constituency the bill was written for

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill drew no cosponsors, so no partisan voting pattern exists in the record; the sole sponsor was the Senate's top Republican.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired power companies
industries.note: The bill would have blocked EPA carbon standards for existing coal plants and eased federal water permitting and oversight of mining discharges, directly protecting coal mining and coal-fired electricity from the regulations they most feared. Its gain would come at the cost of weaker water and air protections for downstream communities.

The bill would strip EPA of its authority to veto Corps permits, remove its ability to disapprove weak state permit programs, and bar reliance on guidance documents, substantially reducing federal environmental enforcement power.
